title: Android to iOS Cross-Reference & Cross-Platform Choices
scopeHtml: Scope: Concept-by-concept mapping, team workflow, Kotlin Multiplatform, Flutter, React Native, shared code, design differences.

notes.title: Baseline and how to read this cross-reference
notes.html:
Android equivalent. This note is the "Rosetta stone" for you as an Android/Kotlin developer: for every concept you already own, the iOS counterpart, the part that does not map, and the decision of when to share code across platforms.

Baseline. Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 minimum target, SwiftUI-first with UIKit essentials, @Observable, NavigationStack, SwiftData, async/await, actors, Swift Testing, Swift Package Manager. Legacy (ObservableObject, Core Data, Combine, XCTest, completion handlers) is "old codebase" material only. New iOS 18/26 items are marked verify.

Three rules of thumb that save weeks.

  1. Do not translate architecture line-by-line; translate intent. A Hilt module is not "an iOS thing", it is "construct your graph at the app root and pass it down".
  2. Value types by default (struct, enum). Where Kotlin used a data class with copy(), Swift uses a struct; classes are for identity, shared mutable state, and Objective-C interop.
  3. The system owns lifecycle and permissions; your code reacts. The iOS app can be suspended within seconds of backgrounding, so "background work" is a budgeted privilege, not a default.

Real industry examples. Airbnb, Uber, Spotify, and Block all run separate Android and iOS teams with shared design systems and shared API contracts, while Dropbox and Square have shared core logic in C++/Kotlin respectively.

Analogy. Moving from Android to iOS is moving from driving on the left to driving on the right: same road rules, same destination, but your reflexes at every junction are subtly wrong for a while.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming "iOS is just Android with different syntax"; the lifecycle, permissions, signing, and distribution models differ materially.
  • Over-claiming Swift knowledge; say what you built, not what you read.
  • Treating Objective-C as irrelevant; many old codebases still mix it (bridging header, @objc).

How some mappings differ in practice.

  • Activity has no iOS twin: the app is a process hosting scenes; a UIViewController is closer to a Fragment than an Activity.
  • Hilt is compile-time graph generation; iOS uses plain initializer injection, @Environment, or runtime containers like Factory and Swinject. No annotation processing.
  • Room entities map to SwiftData @Model classes; Room DAOs map to ModelContext + FetchDescriptor/@Query. See also the persistence notes in this track.

Real examples. Teams at Lyft and Square keep a one-page mapping like this in their onboarding docs, because cross-platform engineers appear frequently.

Analogy. A phrasebook: most phrases translate directly, a few idioms need a whole sentence.

Common interview traps.

  • "Activity is ViewController": they differ because iOS has no OS-driven recreation on rotation; SwiftUI views are re-evaluated, not recreated.
  • Saying SwiftData equals Room: SwiftData is object-graph oriented with change tracking, closer to Core Data than to Room's SQL-first DAOs.
  • Assuming one signing key: iOS needs certificates plus profiles per distribution type.

notes.title: Kotlin Multiplatform sharing business logic with SwiftUI UI
notes.html:
Android equivalent. You already write Kotlin; Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) lets that same module compile to a native iOS framework (via Kotlin/Native) which Swift imports. The usual split: shared commonMain for domain, data (Ktor, SQLDelight, kotlinx.serialization, coroutines), ViewModels optionally; each platform keeps native UI (Compose on Android, SwiftUI on iOS).

 shared/ (KMP module)                           iosApp/ (Xcode)
  commonMain: domain, repository, Ktor, SQLDelight   SwiftUI views -> call shared via generated framework
  androidMain: actual drivers (OkHttp engine)        Shared.xcframework (built by Gradle task / SPM binary)
  iosMain:     actual drivers (Darwin engine)

Consuming a shared Flow from Swift. Raw Kotlin Flow is awkward in Swift, so wrappers or SKIE are used:

// shared/commonMain
class ProfileViewModel(private val repo: UserRepo) {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow<ProfileState>(ProfileState.Loading)
    val state: StateFlow<ProfileState> = _state
    suspend fun load(id: String) { _state.value = ProfileState.Ready(repo.get(id)) }
}
sealed interface ProfileState {
    data object Loading : ProfileState
    data class Ready(val user: User) : ProfileState
}
// Without SKIE: callback-based, manual cancellation
@MainActor @Observable
final class ProfileBridge {
    var text = ""
    private var handle: (any Kotlinx_coroutines_coreFlowCollector)?
    // verify exact generated names: they are ugly (Kotlinx_coroutines_core...)
}

// With SKIE: Flow becomes AsyncSequence, sealed interface becomes exhaustive enum, suspend becomes async
for await state in vm.state {
    switch onEnum(of: state) {          // SKIE helper
    case .loading: text = "..."
    case .ready(let r): text = r.user.name
    }
}
try await vm.load(id: "42")

What SKIE (Touchlab) fixes. Generated Objective-C headers lose type information: sealed classes become unrelated classes (no exhaustive switch), Flow is exposed as Kotlinx_coroutines_coreFlow, suspend functions are callbacks, default arguments disappear, enums with associated data are not enums, and generics are lossy. SKIE adds async/await, AsyncSequence, exhaustive onEnum(of:), and default arguments. Alternatives: KMP-NativeCoroutines (Rick Clephas), manual wrappers, and Kotlin's own direct Swift export (experimental, verify status).

Interop pitfalls.

  • Memory model: the new Kotlin/Native memory manager (default since 1.7.20) removed freeze rules; still, cycles between Kotlin and Swift objects can leak since Kotlin GC and ARC do not see each other (ARC retains from Swift, tracing GC collects Kotlin-side).
  • Threads: Kotlin coroutines on Dispatchers.Main map to the main thread, but Swift 6 @MainActor isolation is not understood by Kotlin; calling Kotlin APIs from @MainActor code is fine, but returning non-Sendable Kotlin types across actors triggers Swift 6 warnings.
  • Build times and framework linking: shipping an XCFramework adds Gradle in the iOS build; CI needs JDK plus Xcode. Teams distribute via Swift Package Manager binary targets or CocoaPods (cocoapods plugin) or direct Xcode "Run Script" phase.
  • Debugging: LLDB on Kotlin frames is limited; stack traces from shared crashes are symbolicated differently (Kotlin/Native dSYM).
  • Exceptions: Kotlin exceptions crossing into Swift terminate the app unless annotated @Throws.
  • Naming: Int becomes Int32, Long becomes Int64, Kotlin Unit becomes KotlinUnit; Boolean becomes KotlinBoolean in generics.
  • Binary size: a KMP framework includes its own runtime and GC (several MB, verify per app).

Who uses it. Cash App (Block), Netflix (studio apps), Philips, Quizlet, Touchlab clients, McDonald's, Forbes. Google officially supports KMP for shared business logic on Android (Jetpack libs such as Room and DataStore have KMP variants, verify coverage).

When it fits. Strong Kotlin team, complex domain/offline sync logic where duplication causes parity bugs, native UI quality matters. When not: tiny app, iOS team with no Kotlin appetite, heavy platform-API-driven code.

Analogy. Two kitchens (Android and iOS) share one prep kitchen (shared module) that cuts the vegetables; each kitchen still plates the dish its own way (UI).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying KMP "writes the app once": it shares logic, not UI (unless Compose Multiplatform).
  • Forgetting @Throws (Kotlin exceptions crash Swift).
  • Treating Flow as free in Swift without SKIE or wrapper.
  • Ignoring that iOS developers must now understand Gradle/Kotlin errors.

notes.title: Compose Multiplatform status (verify)
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Compose Multiplatform (CMP, JetBrains) takes Jetpack Compose's API to iOS, desktop, and web (Wasm). On iOS it draws with Skia (Skiko) into a UIViewController embedded in your app, instead of using UIKit/SwiftUI controls.

Status to verify at interview time: JetBrains announced iOS support as Stable with Compose Multiplatform 1.8.0 (May 2025). Web (Wasm) was Beta at that time. Always confirm on the JetBrains blog before quoting. Capabilities: shared navigation (Navigation Compose KMP port), resources library (compose.components.resources), accessibility mapped to VoiceOver, native-ish scrolling and text editing behaviours, interop with UIKitView (embed UIKit in Compose) and, in the other direction, ComposeUIViewController to host Compose inside SwiftUI.

import SwiftUI
import Shared      // KMP framework

struct ComposeHost: UIViewControllerRepresentable {
    func makeUIViewController(context: Context) -> UIViewController {
        MainViewControllerKt.MainViewController()   // Kotlin: fun MainViewController() = ComposeUIViewController { App() }
    }
    func updateUIViewController(_ vc: UIViewController, context: Context) {}
}

Trade-offs. One UI codebase, but not platform-native: scroll physics, text selection, keyboard handling, accessibility and platform look-and-feel need extra tuning; Liquid Glass (iOS 26) adoption would require manual work (verify). App size grows by the Skia runtime. Good fit for internal tools, dashboards, and teams where Android is the lead platform; weaker for design-led consumer apps.

Real examples. JetBrains' own Toolbox-style apps, Wrike, Forbes, and some fintech teams mixing CMP with native screens; mixed approach (CMP for a feature, SwiftUI for shell) is common.

Analogy. Native UI is local cuisine from each town; CMP is a franchise with one recipe, consistent and efficient, but never exactly the local flavour.

Common interview traps.

  • Quoting "stable" or "beta" without a date and source.
  • Conflating KMP with CMP: KMP is logic, CMP is UI on top of KMP.
  • Ignoring accessibility and platform-gesture differences (swipe-back edge gesture).

notes.title: Flutter and React Native trade-offs versus native
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Compose is a declarative UI toolkit tied to Android; Flutter and React Native are declarative UI toolkits tied to neither platform.

Aspect Native (Kotlin + Swift) Flutter React Native
Language Kotlin, Swift Dart TypeScript/JavaScript
Rendering platform widgets own engine (Impeller, formerly Skia) draws every pixel maps to real native views (New Architecture: Fabric)
Bridge none FFI/platform channels JSI (synchronous C++), TurboModules
New OS features day one wait for plugins wait for libraries/native modules
UI fidelity exact pixel-perfect consistent, not native native components, JS logic
Hiring two specialist pools Dart pool large JS/React pool
Hot reload previews / limited excellent excellent (Fast Refresh)
Performance best near native for UI, startup cost good; heavy lists and animations need care
Code share KMP for logic only ~90 to 100% (UI + logic) ~70 to 95% (UI + logic)
Typical size cost baseline +several MB engine +JS engine (Hermes) and bundle

Numbers on share are folklore; do not quote them as measurements.

Specifics senior engineers cite.

  • React Native's old bridge (JSON async messages) was replaced by the New Architecture (JSI, Fabric, TurboModules); it became the default in React Native 0.76 (late 2024, verify). Expo is now the recommended framework for new projects.
  • Flutter's engine renders via Impeller on iOS (default since Flutter 3.10, verify), which removed shader-compilation jank. Platform views (maps, web views) are the pain point.
  • Both need native modules for deep platform features (widgets, Live Activities, App Intents, HealthKit); those parts are still written in Swift.
  • Over-the-air JS updates (CodePush successor, EAS Update) are possible in RN within App Store rules (no changing core purpose).

Real examples. Discord, Shopify, Microsoft Office, and Coinbase use React Native; Google Pay, BMW, eBay Motors, and Alibaba's Xianyu use Flutter. Airbnb famously moved off React Native back to native in 2018; Instagram, Skype and others have also scaled back or kept hybrid setups.

When to choose what. Startups needing one team and fast iteration: Flutter or RN. Design-driven, deeply platform-integrated or very performance-sensitive consumer app: native. Strong Kotlin org with offline-heavy logic: KMP with native UI. Existing web team: RN.

Analogy. Native is a bespoke suit per customer; Flutter is a uniform made in one factory that fits everyone decently; React Native is a suit made from off-the-rack panels that keep adjusting to each customer's fabric.

Common interview traps.

  • Declaring one "the best": the right answer names constraints (team, time, product).
  • Saying Flutter uses native widgets (it does not) or RN renders in a WebView (it does not).
  • Ignoring maintenance cost: dependency upgrades each OS cycle are the hidden bill.

notes.title: Platform conventions users expect
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Material Design 3 and the system Back gesture. iOS follows the Human Interface Guidelines (HIG); a faithful port that ignores them feels wrong to users even if it "works".

Topic Android users expect iOS users expect
Back system back (gesture or button) swipe from the left edge or the back chevron in the nav bar; no hardware/system back
Navigation drawer, bottom nav, top app bar tab bar (bottom, max 5), navigation bar with title, large titles
Primary action FAB nav-bar button or toolbar; no FAB
Menus overflow 3-dot, bottom sheets context menus (long press), action sheets, confirmationDialog
Dialogs AlertDialog alert (centred, buttons stack)
Share Intent.ACTION_SEND chooser share sheet: ShareLink (SwiftUI) / UIActivityViewController
Permissions runtime dialog, ask in context, rationale single system prompt, one chance; pre-prime with your own screen
Haptics HapticFeedbackConstants, Vibrator UIImpactFeedbackGenerator, .sensoryFeedback modifier (iOS 17)
Pull to refresh SwipeRefreshLayout .refreshable
Settings in-app settings screen in-app plus the Settings.app section for the app
Fonts/icons Roboto, Material Icons San Francisco (Dynamic Type), SF Symbols
Swipe actions usually on long press swipe a row to delete/archive: .swipeActions
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
Text("Hello")
    .font(.body)                       // Dynamic Type scales automatically
Button("Like") { liked.toggle() }
    .sensoryFeedback(.success, trigger: liked)   // iOS 17+
ShareLink(item: url, subject: Text("Check this out"))
Text("Hello", style = MaterialTheme.typography.bodyLarge)  // sp scales with font size
Button(onClick = { liked = !liked; haptic.performHapticFeedback(HapticFeedbackType.LongPress) }) { Text("Like") }
val share = Intent.createChooser(Intent(Intent.ACTION_SEND).apply { type = "text/plain"; putExtra(Intent.EXTRA_TEXT, url) }, null)

Other expectations. Support Dark Mode and Dynamic Type (users set text sizes up to accessibility XXXL). Respect safe areas (notch, Dynamic Island, home indicator). Keyboard avoidance is automatic in SwiftUI. VoiceOver labels (.accessibilityLabel). Edge-swipe back must not be broken by custom gestures; NavigationStack handles it for you. iPad deserves adaptive layout (NavigationSplitView).

Real examples. Apps like Spotify keep brand identity but adopt iOS navigation; Google's own iOS apps (Gmail, Maps) used Material patterns early and moved toward iOS-native chrome (a repeated lesson).

Analogy. Customs and etiquette: tipping rules differ per country; follow them and nobody notices you, break them and everybody does.

Common interview traps.

  • Shipping a FAB, snackbar, or hamburger drawer on iOS.
  • Custom back button hiding the swipe-back gesture.
  • Priming a notification permission too early; with one shot, a denied choice requires a trip to Settings.
  • Ignoring Dynamic Type: clipped layouts and App Review accessibility feedback.

notes.title: Working in a mixed Android and iOS team
notes.html:
Android equivalent. You currently review PRs where "the iOS version does X" is background noise. When you work on both, the job is keeping features and contracts aligned without slowing either team.

Contract first. Agree the API contract before either client builds: OpenAPI/Swagger, GraphQL schema (Apollo clients on both platforms), or protobuf/gRPC. Generate models (OpenAPI Generator emits Kotlin and Swift; Apollo Kotlin/iOS codegen) so field names, nullability and enum cases cannot drift. Version and flag breaking changes; both clients must tolerate unknown enum cases (@unknown default in Swift, else branch in Kotlin).

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
enum Status: String, Codable {
    case active, suspended
    case unknown
    init(from decoder: Decoder) throws {
        let raw = try decoder.singleValueContainer().decode(String.self)
        self = Status(rawValue: raw) ?? .unknown     // forward compatible
    }
}
@Serializable
enum class Status {
    @SerialName("active") ACTIVE,
    @SerialName("suspended") SUSPENDED,
    UNKNOWN
}
val json = Json { coerceInputValues = true }   // unknown values fall back to the default

Release and parity.

  • Feature flags (LaunchDarkly, Firebase Remote Config, Statsig) decouple deploy from release so Android ships Tuesday and iOS ships after App Review.
  • Review latency: Play typically publishes in hours, App Store review commonly takes about a day (verify; it varies), and phased release (7-day) can be paused. Expedited review requests exist for critical fixes.
  • Minimum version policy and a force-update endpoint, because an old iOS binary cannot be rolled back by the server.
  • Parity matrix in the tracker: for each feature, Android status, iOS status, flag, backend dependency. Prefer "same behaviour, platform-native UI".
  • Shared artefacts: design tokens exported to both (Style Dictionary), analytics event schema as a single source (events defined once, codegen per platform), shared test fixtures (golden JSON).
  • Branching: trunk-based with short-lived branches; release trains weekly or biweekly; Fastlane on iOS, Gradle Play Publisher on Android; CI on macOS runners (more expensive and slower than Linux, so cache SPM and DerivedData).

Real examples. Airbnb, Uber and Slack run release trains with flags and an API-schema pipeline; Spotify's squads own a feature across both platforms.

Analogy. Two bands playing the same song: sheet music (contract) must match, tempo (release train) must align, but each band's instruments sound different.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting that iOS releases cannot be hot-rolled back; ship behind flags.
  • Android-only enum assumptions that crash a Swift Codable decoder on unknown cases.
  • Treating "parity" as pixel equality instead of behaviour equality.
  • Underestimating App Review: privacy manifests, data-use declarations and 4.8/3.1.1 can block a release.

notes.title: How to ramp up in iOS in 30, 60 and 90 days
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Think of your Android onboarding: first tiny bug fix, then a feature, then ownership. Same shape, different vocabulary.

Window Goal Concrete work
Days 1 to 30 Fluent in Swift and SwiftUI basics; ship something small Swift language tour (optionals, enums with payloads, protocols, value types, closures, ARC/weak); Stanford CS193p or Apple's "Develop in Swift" tutorials; build a small app (list, detail, network, persistence); fix 2 or 3 low-risk bugs in the team codebase; learn Xcode shortcuts, debugger, Instruments basics
Days 31 to 60 Own a small feature end to end Navigation, state (@Observable), URLSession async + Codable, SwiftData; concurrency (@MainActor, Sendable, task cancellation); unit tests with Swift Testing; UIKit essentials (UIViewControllerRepresentable, lifecycles); handle a crash report with symbolication
Days 61 to 90 Make production-quality decisions Performance (Instruments Time Profiler, Allocations), memory/retain cycles, app lifecycle and background tasks, signing/TestFlight/App Store Connect, accessibility, one release shepherded; review iOS PRs; write a design doc

Study order of Swift topics that trip Android developers. Optionals vs Kotlin nullability (guard let, if let), no data class (structs get memberwise init, Equatable/Hashable synthesized by conformance), protocols with associated types, some/any, property wrappers (@State), result builders (@ViewBuilder), ARC and [weak self] (Kotlin GC hides this), actors and Sendable.

Habits. Read other people's SwiftUI code on GitHub; follow Swift by Sundell, Hacking with Swift, Point-Free; watch WWDC sessions (searchable in the Developer app); pair with the iOS teammate for one PR per week; keep a personal "Android vs iOS" glossary.

Real examples. Many Android engineers at Shopify, Block and Meta crossed over via internal "dual platform" programs; the common bottleneck is not syntax but the lifecycle, signing and App Review mental model.

Analogy. Learning a second instrument: your music theory transfers, your fingers do not.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing a 90-day plan as only "learn Swift"; interviewers want shipped output and review habits.
  • Skipping UIKit: most large production apps still contain it.
  • Saying you will "pick up signing later": it blocks device testing in week one.

notes.title: Design and architecture differences you will feel
notes.html:
Android equivalent. MVVM with Hilt, Repository, UseCases, unidirectional data flow, Navigation graph. iOS has the same ideas under other names, plus a few that go the other way.

  • MVVM with @Observable: the ViewModel is a plain @MainActor @Observable final class; SwiftUI re-renders only views that read changed properties. No collectAsState.
  • TCA (Swift Composable Architecture) by Point-Free: a Redux/MVI-like store with reducers, popular where unidirectional flow and testability matter. Android parallel: MVIKotlin, Orbit, or Circuit.
  • Clean/Modular: SwiftPM local packages per feature (like Gradle modules). Compile times drive modularization decisions on both platforms.
  • DI: no Dagger. Choose between constructor injection (default), @Environment, or Factory / swift-dependencies (Point-Free). Tests swap implementations via protocols.
  • Navigation: SwiftUI NavigationStack(path:) with a typed path is closer to Navigation Compose's route list; coordinators (UIKit era) are the older pattern. Deep links route into the same path.
  • Concurrency: Swift 6 strict concurrency makes data races compile errors, which is stricter than Kotlin; learn Sendable and actor isolation early.
  • Memory: ARC is deterministic; retain cycles with closures are your leak source. Android developers forget [weak self] because GC and viewModelScope hide it.
  • Process model: iOS apps are suspended and may be killed without onDestroy equivalents; persist state eagerly (@SceneStorage, scenePhase).

Real examples. Airbnb's Epoxy (Android) and Lottie (both) show cross-platform parity at the library level; The Browser Company, Pointfree and Mercari have published about TCA and modular SwiftPM.

Analogy. Same orchestral score, different instrument sections: strings (state) and percussion (lifecycle) need different techniques.

Common interview traps.

  • Porting a Hilt-style graph literally instead of using plain initializers.
  • Using a singleton static let shared everywhere (hurts tests).
  • Forgetting scenePhase handling and losing unsaved state.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Map concepts by intent: Activity is not ViewController, Hilt is not a framework you need, Room is not SwiftData, WorkManager is not BGTaskScheduler.
  • KMP shares logic and pairs well with SwiftUI; SKIE removes most interop pain (Flow, sealed types, suspend); mind @Throws, memory cycles, build tooling.
  • Compose Multiplatform for iOS is reported Stable since 1.8.0 (verify date and current version); it is a UI sharing choice with fidelity trade-offs.
  • Flutter and React Native trade native fidelity and day-one APIs for code reuse; platform-specific features still need Swift.
  • Follow HIG conventions (edge-swipe back, tab bar, share sheet, haptics, Dynamic Type); do not port Material patterns.
  • Mixed teams run on contract-first APIs, forward-compatible decoding, feature flags, and a parity matrix.
  • A 30/60/90 plan should end in shipped, reviewed, and measured iOS work, not just reading.
